question.text:
$\qquad$ If you don't water the plants, then they will die.

Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement above?
question.choice1: Water the plants, or they will die.
question.choice2: Don't water the plants, and they won't die.
question.choice3: Either you do not water the plants, or they won't die.
question.choice4: Either you do not water the plants, or they will die.
question.choice5: Water the plants, or they won't die.
question.explanation:
Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

  • $A{:}$ You don't water the plants.

  • $B{:}$ The plants will die.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A \Rightarrow B,$ which is logically equivalent to

\[ \neg A \lor B. \]

The negation of $A$ can be written as

  • $\neg A{:}$ You water the plants.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\qquad$ You water the plants, or the plants will die.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

$\qquad$ Water the plants, or they will die.

question.text: Simplify the statement $\neg \left(X \Rightarrow Y\right).$
question.choice1: $X \land \neg Y$
question.choice2: $X \land Y$
question.choice3: $\neg X \land \neg Y$
question.choice4: $X \lor \neg Y$
question.explanation:
The conditional statement $P \Rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $\neg P \lor Q{:}$

So, in this case, we have the following equivalence:

\[ \neg \left(X \Rightarrow Y\right) \equiv \neg \left(\neg X \lor Y\right) \]

Distributing the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law, we have

\[ \neg \left(\neg X \lor Y\right) \equiv \neg(\neg X) \land \neg Y. \]

Canceling out double negation, we reach

\[ X \land \neg Y. \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $X \land \neg Y.$

So, in this case, we have the following equivalence:

\[ \neg A \Rightarrow B \equiv \neg (\neg A) \lor B \]

Canceling out double negations, we reach

\[ \neg (\neg A) \lor B \equiv A \lor B. \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $A \lor B.$

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $ eg P \Rightarrow Q\equiv P \lor eg Q$
  2. $ eg \left( eg P \Rightarrow Q ight)\equiv eg P \land Q$
  3. $ eg \left( eg P \Rightarrow Q ight)\equiv eg P \land eg Q$
question.choice1: III only
question.choice2: I and III only
question.choice3: I and II only
question.choice4: I only
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of our statements:

  • Statement I is false. Indeed, $\neg P \Rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $\neg(\neg P) \lor Q,$ which in turn is equivalent to $P \lor Q.$

  • Statement II is false, while statement III is true. From part I, we have the following equivalence: \[ \neg P \Rightarrow Q\equiv P \lor Q \] By negating this statement, we get \[ \neg \left(\neg P \Rightarrow Q\right) \equiv \neg \left(P \lor Q\right). \] Distributing the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law, we have \[ \neg \left(P \lor Q\right) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q. \] So, $\neg \left(\neg P \Rightarrow Q\right)$ is equivalent to $\neg P \land \neg Q.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

question.text: Simplify the statement $M \Rightarrow \neg N.$
question.choice1: $\neg(M \land N)$
question.choice2: $M \land N$
question.choice3: $\neg M \lor N$
question.choice4: $M \land \neg N$
question.explanation:
The conditional statement $P \Rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $\neg P \lor Q{:}$

So, in this case, we have the following equivalence:

\[ M \Rightarrow \neg N \equiv \neg M \lor \neg N \]

Using De Morgan's law, we reach

\[ \neg M \lor \neg N \equiv \neg(M \land N). \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $\neg(M \land N).$

question.text: Simplify the statement $ eg( eg A \land B) \Rightarrow eg A.$
question.choice1: $\neg A$
question.choice2: $B \lor A$
question.choice3: $\neg A \land B$
question.choice4: $A \land B$
question.explanation:
First, note that \[ eg( eg A \land B) \Rightarrow eg A \equiv eg ( eg ( eg A \land B)) \lor eg A. \]

Canceling out double negations, we reach \[ eg ( eg ( eg A \land B)) \lor eg A \equiv ( eg A \land B) \lor eg A. \]

Using the commutative law, we have \[ ( eg A \land B) \lor eg A \equiv (B \land eg A ) \lor eg A \]

Finally, by the absorption law, we have

\[ (B \land eg A ) \lor eg A \equiv eg A. \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $ eg A.$

question.text: Simplify the statement $ eg( eg A \vee eg B) \Rightarrow eg A.$
question.choice1: $\neg A \vee \neg B$
question.choice2: $\neg A$
question.choice3: $\neg A \vee B$
question.choice4: $\neg A \wedge \neg B$
question.explanation:
First, note that \[ eg( eg A \vee eg B) \Rightarrow eg A \equiv eg\left( eg( eg A \vee eg B) ight) \vee eg A. \]

Canceling out double negations, we reach \[ eg\left( eg( eg A \vee eg B) ight) \vee eg A \equiv ( eg A \vee eg B) \vee eg A. \]

Using the commutative and associative law, we have \[ ( eg A \vee eg B) \vee eg A \equiv ( eg A \vee eg A) \vee eg B. \]

Finally, by the idempotent law, we have

\[ ( eg A \vee eg A) \vee eg B \equiv eg A \vee eg B. \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $ eg A \vee eg B.$

question.text: Simplify the statement $\neg(P \land Q) \Rightarrow (P \land R).$
question.choice1: $P \land (Q \lor R)$
question.choice2: $P \land (Q \land R)$
question.choice3: $P \lor (Q \lor R)$
question.choice4: $P \land (Q \lor \neg R)$
question.explanation:
First, note that \[ \neg(P \land Q) \Rightarrow (P \land R) \equiv \neg(\neg(P \land Q)) \lor (P \land R). \]

Canceling out double negations, we reach

\[ \neg(\neg(P \land Q)) \lor (P \land R) \equiv (P \land Q) \lor (P \land R). \]

Finally, by the distributive laws, we have

\[ (P \land Q) \lor (P \land R) \equiv P \land (Q \lor R). \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $P \land (Q \lor R).$

question.text: Simplify the statement $\neg (X \land Y) \Rightarrow Y.$
question.choice2: $X \land Y$
question.choice3: $X \lor Y$
question.choice4: $\neg X \lor Y$
question.explanation:
First, note that \[ \neg (X \land Y) \Rightarrow Y \equiv \neg (\neg (X \land Y)) \lor Y. \]

Canceling out double negations, we reach \[ \neg (\neg (X \land Y)) \lor Y \equiv (X \land Y) \lor Y. \]

Finally, by the absorption law, we have

\[ (X \land Y) \lor Y \equiv Y. \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $Y.$

question.text: Simplify the statement $(\neg B \land C) \Rightarrow (B \lor \neg C).$
question.choice1: $B \lor \neg C$
question.choice2: $\neg B \lor C$
question.choice3: $B \land \neg C$
question.choice4: $\neg B \land C$
question.explanation:
First, note that \[ ( eg B \land C) \Rightarrow (B \lor eg C) \equiv eg ( eg B \land C) \lor (B \lor eg C). \]

We can distribute the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law:

\[ eg ( eg B \land C) \lor (B \lor eg C) \equiv ( eg ( eg B) \lor eg C) \lor (B \lor eg C) \]

Canceling out double negations, we reach

\[ ( eg ( eg B) \lor eg C) \lor (B \lor eg C) \equiv (B \lor eg C) \lor (B \lor eg C). \]

Finally, we simplify the disjunction of a statement with itself:

\[ (B \lor eg C) \lor (B \lor eg C) \equiv B \lor eg C \]

So the given statement is equivalent to $B \lor eg C.$
